title: Computer Vision
desc: From pixels to spatial understanding — detection, depth, segmentation, and visual control for intelligent physical systems.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 1 — Introduction to CV
watch.focus: First 30 min. What is an image tensor, why CV is hard, the gap between pixels and meaning.

concept.title: Cameras turn light into numbers
concept.body:
A digital camera measures light intensity at each sensor location. The result is a tensor of shape H×W×C. A 224×224 RGB image = 150,528 numbers.

Spatial filtering (convolution with a kernel): blur with Gaussian, detect edges with Sobel, sharpen with Laplacian. Modern CNNs learn these filters — understanding classical ones gives you intuition for what your model does.
concept.analogy: A camera is a light measurement device. Each pixel asks: 'how many photons hit me?' The answer is a number. Your model gets millions of these numbers and must extract meaning.

challenge.q: You apply Gaussian blur before edge detection. Most likely effect?

opts.t: Edges sharpen — Gaussian enhances high-frequency features
Edge detection degrades — blurring removes high-frequency edge information
Edges more accurate — noise removed with edges

challenge.hint: Edges are high-frequency features. Gaussian is a low-pass filter.
challenge.exp: Gaussian blur removes high-frequency content — including edges. This is why preprocessing choices matter: you may remove signal along with noise.

project.title: Classical Filter Toolkit
project.desc: Build a reusable image processing toolkit across three domains: natural, medical, robotics.
deliverables: Implement: Gaussian blur, Sobel edges, Laplacian sharpening (numpy)
Apply to: natural RGB image, chest X-ray, robot depth frame
Side-by-side visualization for all three domains
README: which filters suit each domain and why?
project.hint: scipy.signal.convolve2d or manual numpy. PIL/OpenCV to load. matplotlib to display.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 8 — Spatial Localization (first 20 min)
watch.focus: How classical features motivated deep learning. Why hand-crafted features were limited.

concept.title: Describing patches before deep learning
concept.body:
HOG: gradient histograms, used in pedestrian detection. SIFT: scale/rotation invariant keypoints. ORB: fast binary descriptor — still used in real-time SLAM systems where speed matters more than accuracy.

CNNs replaced HOG/SIFT for most tasks. Understanding classical features gives you intuition for what deep layers discover.
concept.analogy: Classical features manually measure face properties (nose width, eye distance). Deep learning learns its own measurements — but knowing manual ones helps you understand what the network discovers.
concept.visual:
HOG pipeline:
Image → gradient magnitude/direction
→ local cell histograms → block normalization
→ feature vector

ORB = oriented keypoints + binary BRIEF descriptors

challenge.q: A robot localizing in a plain white corridor needs to match views to a map. Which detector performs worst?

opts.t: All classical detectors — need corners/edges/texture to find keypoints

challenge.hint: Classical detectors need gradient variation. What happens on uniform surfaces?
challenge.exp: All classical detectors fail in low-texture environments — plain walls have no corners or gradients. This is why deep learning or LiDAR is preferred for SLAM in structured indoor environments like hospitals or warehouses.

project.title: Feature Matching Pipeline
project.desc: Build a classical feature matching pipeline and test its limits.
deliverables: Extract ORB keypoints from two views of same scene
Match with BFMatcher + Lowe ratio test, visualize
Apply to: textured outdoor scene (works) vs low-texture indoor (fails)
Quantify: correct matches per case
README: when classical vs deep features for your robotics/medical work?
project.hint: cv2.ORB_create(), detectAndCompute(), BFMatcher. Ratio test: keep where dist1/dist2 < 0.75.

watch.title: MIT 6.8300 Lec 2 — Image Formation (free OCW)
watch.focus: Pinhole camera model, intrinsic matrix K, projection from 3D world to 2D pixel.

concept.title: How 3D world becomes 2D image
concept.body: Every camera: p = K [R|t] P. K = intrinsic matrix (focal length, principal point). [R|t] = extrinsic matrix (camera pose). Non-negotiable for robotics CV: depth estimation, stereo, visual odometry, 3D reconstruction all depend on this.
concept.analogy: K is the camera's personality — fixed focal length, principal point. [R|t] is where you place it in the world. Together they tell you where any 3D point lands on your sensor.
concept.visual:
p = K · [R|t] · P
K = [[fx,  0, cx],
     [ 0, fy, cy],
     [ 0,  0,  1]]
u = fx·X/Z + cx
v = fy·Y/Z + cy

challenge.q: Camera: f=500px, point at Z=2m, X=0.5m right of optical axis. Pixel displacement from center?
challenge.exp: 500 × 0.5/2 = 125 px. This formula governs all stereo, depth, and odometry calculations.

project.title: Camera Calibration & Projection
project.desc: Calibrate a real camera. Project 3D points, verify with ground truth.
deliverables: Calibrate using OpenCV chessboard or KITTI calibration files
Project 3D points → image, compare with GT pixel positions
Visualize: reprojection error per point
Undistort image using calibration parameters
README: what does K tell you about your camera?
project.hint: cv2.calibrateCamera(), cv2.projectPoints(). KITTI includes calibration files if no chessboard.

assignment.title: Classical Vision Pipeline
assignment.desc: Full pipeline: calibrate, extract features, match views, estimate relative camera pose.
deliverables: Camera calibration and undistortion
ORB feature extraction + matching with ratio test
Essential matrix estimation from matched points
Decompose E → R and t (relative camera pose)
Visualize: matched features + camera motion direction
README: map each classical component to its modern deep equivalent
assignment.hint: OpenCV: calibrateCamera → undistort → ORB → BFMatcher → findEssentialMat → recoverPose.

units.title: CNNs — How and Why They Work

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 5 — Convolutional Neural Networks
watch.focus: Full ~70 min. Why spatial structure matters, receptive fields, pooling, weight sharing. This is the core.

concept.title: Learning filters, not hand-crafting them
concept.body: Classical CV: you design filters. CNNs: data decides. Receptive field: how much of the original image influences one neuron — grows with depth. Early layers detect edges. Deep layers detect objects. Weight sharing: one filter everywhere — translation invariant.
concept.analogy: Classical CV hires specialists for every task. CNNs hire generalists who learn the best tools for YOUR specific data.
concept.visual:
RF grows by (k-1) per layer for k×k kernels:
1 layer(3×3): RF=3
5 layers(3×3): RF=11

Layer hierarchy:
L1: edges, colors
L2: corners, textures
L3: parts (eyes, wheels)
L4+: objects, scenes

challenge.q: CNN has 5 conv layers, each 3×3, stride=1. Receptive field of layer 5 neuron?
challenge.exp: 1 + 5×2 = 11×11. Deep networks needed for large objects — many layers for RF to cover the full object.

project.title: CNN Feature Visualizer
project.desc: Train a small CNN from scratch. Visualize what each layer learns.
deliverables: Train 4-layer CNN on CIFAR-10 (~85% accuracy)
Visualize learned filters in layer 1 (should show edges/colors)
Feature maps for a specific input across all layers
Grad-CAM on 5 test images
README: does the hierarchy (edges→parts→objects) appear in your visualizations?
project.hint: torchvision.utils.make_grid for filters. Forward hooks to capture feature maps.

units.title: Modern Architectures
units.meta: ResNet, DenseNet, ViT — when to use what

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 9 — CNN Architectures
watch.focus: ResNet skip connections (mathematical reason), DenseNet, ViT overview. ~50 min.

concept.title: Architecture design as engineering decisions
concept.body: ResNet: output = F(x)+x. Skip connections solve vanishing gradients. Dominates medical imaging. DenseNet: each layer connects to ALL previous layers. Max feature reuse. Strong for scarce data. ViT: patches as tokens, self-attention, no inductive bias — needs large data.
concept.analogy: ResNet: highway with emergency lanes. DenseNet: everyone talks to everyone. ViT: global meeting where every patch attends to every other simultaneously.
concept.visual:
ResNet block:
x → [Conv-BN-ReLU-Conv-BN] → (+x) → ReLU

DenseNet layer n:
x_n = F([x_0, x_1, ..., x_{n-1}])

ViT:
patches → embeddings → transformer × N → class token

challenge.q: 1,500 labeled chest X-rays. Best starting architecture?

opts.t: DenseNet-121 pretrained — gold standard for chest X-ray (CheXNet)
ResNet-18 from scratch — simpler is better
All perform identically on small datasets

challenge.hint: DenseNet-121 is the CheXNet architecture. ViT needs more fine-tuning data than ResNet families.
challenge.exp: DenseNet-121 pretrained is the gold standard for chest X-ray (CheXNet paper). Dense connections are a built-in regularizer for small datasets. ViT needs large pretraining to generalize. From scratch is worst — 1,500 images cannot learn representations from random init.

project.title: Architecture Benchmark on Medical Images
project.desc: Benchmark ResNet-18, DenseNet-121, ViT-tiny on a medical dataset.
deliverables: Fine-tune all three on NIH Chest X-ray mini split
Training curves, final AUROC, inference time, parameter count
Grad-CAM (ResNet/DenseNet) vs attention maps (ViT) on same images
Table: accuracy vs compute vs parameters
README: which would you deploy clinically and why?
project.hint: timm library has all three. Same hyperparameters for fair comparison. Freeze backbone first, then unfreeze.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 7 — Training Neural Networks II
watch.focus: LR schedules, batch normalization intuition, regularization strategies. ~60 min.

concept.title: The engineering of making models learn
concept.body: Transfer learning: start from ImageNet weights — model already knows edges, textures, shapes. Fine-tune for your domain. Critical for medical (small datasets). Medical augmentation: careful — don't flip in ways that change clinical meaning. Focal loss: for class imbalance (common in medical).
concept.analogy: Transfer learning: hiring someone who already knows how to drive and teaching them your city's roads. Training from scratch: teaching someone who has never seen a road.
concept.visual:
Fine-tuning strategy:
1. Freeze backbone, train head (few epochs)
2. Unfreeze last few layers, lower LR
3. Unfreeze all, very low LR (optional)

Focal loss: -α(1-pt)^γ · log(pt)
γ>0 downweights easy examples

challenge.q: Classifier: 95% accuracy, AUROC=0.61. Dataset: 90% normal, 10% pneumonia. Problem?

opts.t: Class imbalance — model predicts "normal" always, achieving 90% accuracy trivially
Transfer learning is hurting — train from scratch

challenge.hint: If 90% are normal, predicting "normal" always gives 90% accuracy. What does AUROC=0.61 reveal?
challenge.exp: Predicting "normal" always achieves 90% accuracy but AUROC≈0.5. Your 0.61 shows barely above random. Fix: weighted CE or focal loss, oversample minority class, use AUROC as primary metric not accuracy.

project.desc: Train on deliberately imbalanced medical data. Compare loss functions.
deliverables: Create 90/10 imbalanced split (normal/pneumonia)
Train: standard CE, weighted CE, focal loss
Compare: accuracy, AUROC, F1, precision-recall curve for each
Best threshold at 0.9 sensitivity from PR curve
README: what metric should you use for imbalanced medical data?
project.hint: torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=...) for weighted CE. sklearn for AUROC, F1.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 11 — Detection and Segmentation (first 35 min)
watch.focus: Detection evolution: sliding windows → R-CNN → Faster R-CNN → YOLO. Why each step was needed.

concept.title: From classification to localization
concept.body:
Faster R-CNN: RPN proposes regions, classifier refines. Accurate, ~5fps. YOLO: one-pass grid prediction, real-time. For robotics: YOLO. For medical (accuracy critical): Faster R-CNN or YOLO with careful NMS tuning.

IoU = overlap/union. NMS: keep highest-confidence, remove duplicates.
concept.analogy: Faster R-CNN: security guard who first flags suspicious areas, then examines each carefully. YOLO: surveillance camera processing the entire scene in one glance.
concept.visual:
IoU = |A∩B|/|A∪B|  (0=no overlap, 1=perfect)
NMS: sort by confidence
→ keep if IoU < threshold with all kept boxes
mAP = mean Average Precision across IoU thresholds

challenge.q: YOLOv8 misses occluded instrument 30% of frames; Faster R-CNN misses only 8%. Why?

opts.t: YOLO is slower so it skips frames
Faster R-CNN two-stage process allows careful per-region analysis of difficult cases
Faster R-CNN uses larger input resolution by default

challenge.hint: What does two-stage processing allow that single-pass cannot?
challenge.exp: Two-stage detectors dedicate a full classification pass per proposed region — more thorough on difficult/occluded cases. For safety-critical surgical robotics, accuracy-speed tradeoff often favors accuracy.

project.title: Surgical Instrument Detector
project.desc: Deploy YOLOv8 on a surgical or medical instrument video.
deliverables: Run YOLOv8 on surgical tool video (YouTube or CholecT50 dataset)
Boxes, class labels, confidence per frame
Log: detection rate per class, confidence distribution, missed frames
Failure analysis: occlusion, lighting, fast motion
README: would you deploy this in a real OR? What needs to change?
project.hint: pip install ultralytics. model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt"). model.track(source="video.mp4") for video.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 11 — Segmentation (from 35 min)
watch.focus: FCN, UNet skip connections, instance vs semantic segmentation difference.

concept.title: Pixel-level understanding
concept.body: UNet: encoder (compress) + decoder (expand) + skip connections preserving spatial detail. Critical for medical imaging where precise boundaries matter. Mask R-CNN: Faster R-CNN + mask prediction branch. Detects + classifies + segments simultaneously.
concept.analogy: Detection = rectangle around a country. Segmentation = coloring every pixel precisely, respecting every coastline. UNet's skip connections keep the high-resolution blueprint while building the compressed overview.
concept.visual:
UNet:
Encoder: 572→286→143→72→36
Decoder: 36→72→143→286→572
Skip: copy+concat encoder features at each scale
→ preserves fine spatial detail

challenge.q: UNet retinal vessels: Dice=0.91 (thick), Dice=0.43 (thin, 1-2px). Most likely cause?

opts.t: Class imbalance — thin vessels are tiny pixel fraction, loss dominated by background
Skip connections are causing this — remove them

challenge.hint: How much of the image is 1-2px thin vessels vs background?
challenge.exp: Extreme class imbalance. Thin vessels occupy very few pixels — standard loss ignores them. Fix: weighted loss upweighting thin vessel pixels, or topology-aware loss penalizing missed thin structures.

project.title: Retinal Vessel Segmentation
project.desc: Train UNet for retinal vessels. Handle thin structure challenge.
deliverables: Train UNet on DRIVE retinal vessel dataset (20 training images)
Compare: standard Dice loss vs weighted Dice (upweight thin vessels)
Dice score per vessel thickness category
Visualization: prediction overlay, error map (thin vs thick vessels)
README: what does this tell you about loss design for medical imaging?
project.hint: segmentation-models-pytorch. DRIVE dataset is free. Compute vessel thickness with distance transform for loss weighting.

secondary_watch.title: AI for Medicine Specialization — Course 1: AI for Medical Diagnosis
secondary_watch.focus: Week 2-3: segmentation evaluation metrics (Dice coefficient, IoU), class imbalance handling, UNet architecture for medical images, soft Dice loss. These fill a specific gap: clinical evaluation metrics and loss functions used in medical image segmentation that CS231N does not cover.

watch.title: SORT paper abstract + intro (15 min read)
watch.focus: Core idea: Kalman filter (motion prediction) + IoU matching (Hungarian algorithm). The simplest effective tracker.

concept.title: Identity across time
concept.body: SORT: Kalman predicts next position, Hungarian algorithm matches predictions to detections by IoU. DeepSORT: adds appearance features for occlusion and re-entry. When objects cross, appearance helps re-assign IDs.
concept.analogy: SORT: predict where your friend is walking, check if anyone nearby matches. DeepSORT: also check what your friend is wearing — useful when people cross paths.
concept.visual:
SORT per frame:
1. Kalman predict → expected positions
2. Detect → new bounding boxes
3. Hungarian match: predictions↔detections by IoU
4. Update matched, create new, delete lost (>max_age)

challenge.q: SORT loses surgical instrument for 3 frames (occluded). It reappears. What happens to its ID?

opts.t: ID preserved — SORT remembers across occlusions
ID may change — track deleted after max_age, reappearing object gets new ID
SORT pauses and resumes with same ID

challenge.hint: SORT deletes tracks after max_age missed frames. What happens on reappearance?
challenge.exp: Track deleted after max_age frames — reappearing instrument gets a new ID (identity switch). Fix: increase max_age or use DeepSORT's appearance features for re-identification.

project.title: Instrument Tracker with Identity
project.desc: Implement SORT on your surgical detector. Measure identity switches.
deliverables: Implement SORT: Kalman filter + Hungarian matching
Annotate tracks with consistent colors and IDs
Detect and log identity switches
Compare: SORT with max_age=1 vs max_age=5
README: how often does ID switch? What would fix it for a real surgical robot?
project.hint: filterpy for Kalman. scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment for Hungarian matching.

assignment.desc: Detect, segment, and track all instruments simultaneously. Portfolio-grade.

watch.title: MIT 6.8300 Lec 4 — Stereo and Depth
watch.focus: Epipolar constraint, disparity computation, depth = fB/d derivation.

concept.title: Two cameras, one depth
concept.body: Epipolar geometry: a point in the left image lies on a known line in the right image — reduces 2D search to 1D. Disparity d = horizontal shift. depth = f·B/d. More disparity = closer. Point cloud: convert depth map to 3D (x,y,z) per pixel.
concept.analogy: Your two eyes give depth perception. Close one — the world flattens. Closer objects shift more between your two views — that shift IS depth information.
concept.visual:
Disparity: d = u_left - u_right
Depth: Z = f·B/d
f=focal length, B=baseline between cameras

Large disparity → small depth (close)
Small disparity → large depth (far)

challenge.q: Stereo: B=0.12m, f=600px. Object A: d=60px. Object B: d=6px. Which is closer and depths?

project.title: Stereo Depth Pipeline
deliverables: KITTI stereo pair → disparity with OpenCV StereoSGBM
Disparity → depth map using f and B from calibration
Project to 3D point cloud (x,y,z per pixel)
Visualize with Open3D, color-coded by depth
README: what does the robot now know that it didn't from a 2D image?
project.hint: cv2.StereoSGBM_create(). KITTI calib files give f and B. open3d.geometry.PointCloud for visualization.

watch.title: Depth Anything V2 blog post + NeRF abstract (10 min)
watch.focus: How self-supervised monocular depth works (photometric loss). What NeRF does conceptually.

concept.title: 3D from one camera
concept.body: Monocular depth: predict depth from single image using learned priors. Self-supervised: adjacent frames + camera motion → photometric reconstruction loss. No labels needed. DepthAnything / MiDaS: foundation models. Strong zero-shot but needs domain fine-tuning. NeRF: learns 3D scene from multiple views, synthesizes novel viewpoints.
concept.analogy: Monocular depth: one eye, using learned experience about depth cues. NeRF: memorize an entire 3D scene so well you can recreate any view from any angle.
concept.visual:
Self-supervised monocular:
Frame t + Frame t+1 + pose network
→ warp t using predicted depth+pose
→ photometric loss with t+1
→ no depth labels needed

challenge.q: DepthAnything fine-tuned outdoors, deployed in surgical scene. Fails. Specific challenge beyond distribution shift?

opts.t: Shiny metallic instruments violate Lambertian assumption — specular reflections confuse photometric loss

challenge.hint: Self-supervised depth assumes surfaces reflect diffusely. What are surgical instruments made of?
challenge.exp: Shiny metallic surfaces violate the Lambertian assumption — highlights move with viewpoint, not geometry. Photometric consistency breaks on surgical instruments. This is an open problem in surgical CV.

Visualize depth maps, assess failure modes per domain

Fine-tune on 20 target domain samples, measure improvement
README: what does the domain gap mean for your application?
project.hint: DepthAnything v2 on HuggingFace. Even qualitative analysis is valuable.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 12 — first 20 min on optical flow
watch.focus: What optical flow is, Lucas-Kanade intuition, why dense flow matters for video understanding.

concept.title: Seeing motion as a field
concept.body: Optical flow: for every pixel, estimate (u,v) motion to next frame. RAFT: deep, iterative refinement, state of the art. For robotics: separate camera ego-motion from object motion. Background flow = ego-motion. Anomalous flow = moving obstacles.
concept.analogy: Optical flow is the velocity map of your image. Every pixel gets an arrow showing where it moved. Decode which arrows come from camera motion vs actual objects moving.
concept.visual:
Forward camera motion → radial outward flow from FOE
Moving object → flow different from background
Dense flow: H×W×2 (u,v per pixel)
RAFT: 12 iterative refinement steps

challenge.q: Hospital robot moving forward detects anomalous optical flow in lower-right of frame. What does this indicate?

opts.t: Moving object (person, cart) in that region — different from expected ego-motion pattern

challenge.hint: Background = predictable radial ego-motion. What causes a region to differ?
challenge.exp: Anomalous flow = independent object motion. Principle behind optical-flow obstacle detection: compute expected ego-motion, subtract, flag residual motion as moving obstacles.

project.title: Motion Segmentation for Navigation
project.desc: Compute optical flow. Segment moving obstacles from static background.
deliverables: Dense optical flow with RAFT on robot navigation video
Segment: moving objects (high residual flow) vs static background
Visualize: flow field as arrows + motion mask overlaid on video
README: how would you integrate this into a robot safety system?
project.hint: torchvision.models.optical_flow has RAFT. Flow magnitude = sqrt(u²+v²). Background ≈ median flow direction.

watch.title: Cyrill Stachniss SLAM lecture (first 25 min)
watch.focus: What is SLAM, why VO drifts, what loop closure does. Conceptual foundation.

concept.title: Where am I? Using only images.
concept.body: Visual odometry: estimate camera trajectory from image sequences. Chain R,t estimates → full trajectory. Drift: small errors accumulate. Loop closure: detect revisited places, correct accumulated error. Classical VO: ORB keypoints → essential matrix → R,t.
concept.analogy: Walking blindfolded, counting steps and turns. Each small counting error adds up (drift). If you recognize a landmark you've seen before, you can correct your position (loop closure).
concept.visual:
VO pipeline:
Frame t, t+1 → keypoints → match
→ Essential matrix E → R, t
→ chain: T_{t+1} = T_t · [R|t]
Drift: ε per step → O(n·ε) total error

challenge.q: VO drift: indoors 0.5%, outdoors 8%. Most likely cause?

opts.t: Outdoor scenes have more moving objects
Outdoor: large illumination and scale changes — keypoints become inconsistent across frames
VO only works with stereo cameras outdoors

challenge.hint: What makes keypoint matching harder outdoors: dynamic lighting, shadows, large depth range.
challenge.exp: Outdoor: dynamic lighting, large depth variation, greater frame-to-frame texture changes → less reliable keypoint matching → more per-frame error. Indoor: controlled lighting, static objects, known scale.

project.desc: Implement classical VO on KITTI. Visualize drift. Quantify ATE.
deliverables: ORB keypoints, match with ratio test
Essential matrix estimation, decompose to R and t

Plot estimated vs GT trajectory (top-down view)
Compute ATE (Absolute Trajectory Error)
README: where does drift appear? What would loop closure fix?
project.hint: KITTI sequence 00. cv2.findEssentialMat(pts1, pts2, K), cv2.recoverPose(E,...).

assignment.desc: Optical flow + visual odometry = unified visual navigation module.

watch.title: Hendrycks & Dietterich 2019 — abstract + intro (10 min read)
watch.focus: Corruption types, mCE computation, why robustness matters for deployment.

concept.title: Does your model survive the real world?
concept.body: Trained on clean images, deployed facing noise, blur, weather, sensor degradation. mCE: mean Corruption Error across 15 corruption types × 5 severities. Medical: scanner noise, motion artifacts, cross-site variation. Robotics: rain, dust, lighting changes.
concept.analogy: Testing CV only on clean images is like testing a car only in a sunny parking lot. Real deployment means rain, night, construction zones, and unexpected conditions.
concept.visual:
Corruptions: Gaussian noise, blur, fog, brightness,
JPEG, pixelate, elastic transform...
mCE = mean over corruptions of (error / AlexNet baseline)
Lower mCE = more robust

challenge.q: Medical classifier: ECE=0.04 (clean). After Gaussian noise severity=3: ECE=0.21. What does this reveal?

opts.t: Calibration breaks under corruption — model stays confident exactly when it should be uncertain

challenge.hint: Rising ECE under corruption: confidence vs actual accuracy — what is the relationship?
challenge.exp: Model stays confident even as accuracy drops — worst deployment scenario: fails while appearing reliable. A trustworthy model should show INCREASING uncertainty under corruption.

project.title: Robustness Profile
project.desc: Complete robustness profile for your medical classifier.
deliverables: 5 corruption types × 3 severities using albumentations
Accuracy + ECE at each corruption × severity combination
Heatmap: corruption type (rows) × severity (cols) → accuracy
Identify worst-case corruption for your model
README: which corruptions are most clinically realistic for your setting?
project.hint: albumentations: GaussNoise, MotionBlur, RandomFog. sns.heatmap for the corruption heatmap.

watch.title: Hendrycks & Gimpel 2017 — abstract + section 2 (15 min read)
watch.focus: Why max softmax fails for OOD, what AUROC measures in this context.

concept.title: Knowing what you have not seen
concept.body: A chest X-ray model will silently misclassify a knee MRI — with high confidence. Max softmax: fails — trained to be confident regardless. Energy score: E(x) = -log Σ exp(fᵢ(x)), theoretically grounded. Mahalanobis: distance from input to class-conditional feature distributions — best empirically.
concept.analogy: A cardiologist trained only in cardiology should say 'I don't know' when shown a dermatology case. OOD detection gives your model the ability to say 'I don't know'.
concept.visual:
Max softmax: max(softmax(logits))  ← overconfident on OOD
Energy: -log Σ exp(f_i(x))  ← theoretically grounded
Mahalanobis: min_c (z-μ_c)ᵀ Σ⁻¹(z-μ_c)  ← best empirically

challenge.q: AUROC: max softmax=0.64, energy=0.88, Mahalanobis=0.91. Same model. Why does Mahalanobis win without retraining?

opts.t: Uses feature space geometry — detects inputs far from training clusters regardless of output confidence

challenge.exp: Mahalanobis measures distance from training class clusters in penultimate feature space — rich representation of what the model knows. OOD inputs far from all clusters are flagged regardless of softmax confidence.
